messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arun, a 42‑year‑old farmer in rural Mississippi, grew up on his family’s farm, where the rhythm of planting and harvesting is measured by the sun and the weather. He is married to Maya, a schoolteacher, and they have three children. The event that has come to dominate his life occurred when Arun’s youngest son, Kiran, was only nine and was suddenly taken to the county hospital with a severe, life‑threatening infection that clamped his throat and lungs. The doctors said his airway was obstructed and that he might need a tracheostomy. Arun was left alone in the dim, fluorescent‑lit waiting room as a nurse placed a nasopharyngeal tube over Kiran’s swollen throat. The nurse played the lullaby “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star” from a portable speaker, the tune drifting through the stale air. That night, as the song floated through the hallway, Arun watched, in that small, flickering light, the tightness around Kiran’s neck, the pallor of his lips, and the red streak of a tiny blood drop on the nurse’s hand. When the boy’s breathing finally steadied, the nurse whispered that the procedure had been a success, but Arun’s heart still clenched around that image. The next morning, the memory of the hospital’s fluorescent glow and the song began to surface on its own, a sudden flash that left Arun breathless. He found himself looking for the image of Kiran’s neck, noticing any constriction of a throat or swelling of a wound, and hearing any song that carried the same rhythm. The more he watched for those visual signs, the more his mind chased them into the dark corners of his bedroom, where the blinds were drawn and the night lights off. The darkness, in turn, amplified his fear that something similar could happen again, a sense that the child’s breathing might be strangled once more. When the house fell silent, Arun’s thoughts would spiral, and he would feel as though he were back in that waiting room, with his son’s throat tightening. The images came not as a steady replay but as brief, disjointed fragments that would appear without warning and vanish before he could fully process them. Because each night’s darkness seemed to beckon the memory, Arun began to avoid sleeping in his own bed. He stayed up past midnight, scrolling through pictures of his farm, listening to the radio’s playlist of old country songs that, when the same melody played, would trigger a rush of fear. He also avoided the company of others, believing that if he were alone with the house, he would be safe from those “people who might bring a song or a touch that would remind him of the throat.” His avoidance of people extended to his usual weekly market trip, where he would leave his truck in the shade and wait for the next vendor, refusing to walk past the store’s front. His attempts to delay sleep, to stay awake and keep his mind occupied, only reinforced the idea that the darkness at night was a portal for danger. The more he stayed awake, the longer the nights lasted, and the more he felt the need to postpone going to bed, as if sleep itself were a threat. In the weeks that followed, the cycle tightened. Every time he saw a swollen arm or a painful bruise, he recalled the hospital’s tight bandage and felt the memory rush back, its intensity amplified by the dimness of his barn shed at dusk. The more he tried to escape that feeling, the more he found himself on the edge of sleep, avoiding both the dark and the company of others. The isolation at work became palpable when, during a harvest, a co‑worker mentioned a new safety protocol that included a short pause for rest. Arun declined, saying he did not need a break, because he feared the rest period would give him time to imagine a child's throat tightening. The result was a growing sense of detachment from his wife and a decline in his farm’s productivity, as he spent fewer hours tending to the fields and more hours alone, staring at the flickering porch light. The turning point came when Arun’s wife noticed he had missed their son’s recital, citing “I was too tired” and “the lights scared me.” She begged him to seek help, arguing that the fear was not only hurting their family but also the livelihood they had worked so hard to maintain. It was that night, after staying up until dawn listening to the same song that had once comforted a hospital patient, that Arun finally realized the cycle was unsustainable. He feared that the night would bring another intrusion, that another song might set his mind ablaze, and that he would keep drifting further from the people he loved and the work that gave him purpose. The hope that kept him in the session now was that he could break the loop, reclaim his nights, and restore the quiet confidence that once defined him as a husband, father, and farmer.
